paragraphs.text: Or, for Asaph; David’s melancholy psalm some call it, made by him when he was in grievous affliction and desertion. Out of which he seeketh to wind by earnest prayer, by deep meditation upon God’s former favours and unchangeable nature; and, lastly, by calling to mind God’s wondrous works of old, both in proving and in preserving his Church and chosen.
paragraphs.anchor: A Psalm of Asaph

paragraphs.text: I prayed instantly and constantly, and sped accordingly. No faithful prayer is ineffectual.
paragraphs.anchor: I cried unto God with my voice, &c.

paragraphs.text: The time of affliction is the time of supplication, Psa 50:15.
paragraphs.anchor: In the day of my trouble

paragraphs.text: Heb. My hand was poured out; that is, stretched out in prayer; or wet with continual weeping. Non fuit remissa, nec retracta in lectum.
paragraphs.anchor: My sore ran in the night

paragraphs.text: Or, was not tired; in allusion, belike, to Moses’s hands held up against Amalek; though
paragraphs.anchor: And ceased not

paragraphs.text: I prayed on, though I had little heart to do it (as Daniel afterwards did the king’s work, though he were sick), or though with much infirmity, while I rather wrangled with God, by cavilling objections, than wrestled with him, as I ought to have done; by important prayer.
paragraphs.anchor: My soul refused to be comforted

paragraphs.text: Tumultuabar, fluctuando perstrepebam; for God seemed to be angry, and to cast out my prayers; this made me mourn, and little less than murmur.
paragraphs.anchor: I remembered God, and was troubled

paragraphs.text: With sense of sin and fear of wrath. This was a very grievous and dangerous temptation, such as we must pray not to be led into, or at least not be left under, lest we utterly despair.
paragraphs.anchor: My spirit was overwhelmed

paragraphs.text: Thou holdest the watches of mine eyes, that is, mine eyebrows, saith the Chaldee, so that I can neither sleep nor speak. Job complaineth of the like misery, Job 7:8 See Psa 38:10
paragraphs.anchor: Thou holdest mine eyes waking

paragraphs.text: Curae leves loquuntur, ingentes stupent.
paragraphs.anchor: That I cannot speak

paragraphs.text: What thou didst for Adam, Abraham, Israel, in Egypt, &c., all which was written purposely, that we, through patience and comfort of the Scriptures, might have hope. See Deu 32:7.
paragraphs.anchor: I have considered the days of old

paragraphs.text: i.e. My former feelings and experiments, being glad, in this scarcity of comfort, to live upon the old store, as bees do in winter.
paragraphs.anchor: I call to remembrance my song in the night

paragraphs.text: Psa 4:4, see there.
paragraphs.anchor: I commune with mine own heart

paragraphs.text: For the cause and cure of my present distempers.
paragraphs.anchor: And my spirit made diligent search

paragraphs.text: No, nor at all, though the extremity and length of the psalmist’s grief put him upon these sad interrogatories, with some diffidence, touching the nature and promise of God.
paragraphs.anchor: Will the Lord cast off for ever?

paragraphs.text: So the devil and carnal reason would have persuaded him; and did haply for a time. But this very questioning the matter showeth he yet lay languishing at hope’s hospital, waiting for comfort. The soul may successively doubt, and yet believe.
paragraphs.anchor: Will he be favourable no more?

paragraphs.text: They that go down into the pit (of despair) cannot hope for God’s truth, Isa 38:18, but so doth not any saint in his deepest desertions.
paragraphs.anchor: Is his mercy clean gone for ever?

paragraphs.text: Hath he retracted his promises, recalled his oracles confirmed with oath, seal? No, he will not suffer his faithfulness to fail, nor alter the thing that is gone out of his mouth, Psa 89:33.
paragraphs.anchor: Doth his promise fail for evermore?

paragraphs.text: So it seemeth sometimes to those that are long afflicted and short-spirited; but what saith the prophet? Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, they may prove unnatural, and grow out of kind, as Medea, and those Suevian women (Heyl. Geog.), who threw their young children at the Romans, under the conduct of Drusus, son-in-law to Augustus, instead of darts, yet God will not forget his people, Isa 49:15. Indeed, he can as soon forget himself, and change his nature.
paragraphs.anchor: Hath God forgotten to be gracious?

paragraphs.text: These things the psalmist speaketh not as utterly despairing, but as one courageously, wrestling against an old manslayer, and a misgiving heart of his own. Homines vero securi, et voluptatibus ebrii, nihil horum intelllgunt. This is little understood by profane sensualists, who, therefore, reap no great benefit by the reading of these psalms.
paragraphs.anchor: Hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies?

paragraphs.text: My frailty and folly. Here he begins to recollect, and recall himself, as every good soul will, after its extravagancies and outbursts. Vatablus rendereth it, Mors mea est, This is my death; Beza, Caedes mea haec, This is my death wound, sc. whereof I should surely die, were it not for the change of God’s hand upon me.
paragraphs.anchor: And I said, This is my infirmity

paragraphs.text: This is supplied out of the following verse. Some make no such supply, but render the text thus, The right hand of the Most High can change these things. Others, This is the change of the right hand of the Most High, and is therefore to be taken patiently; shall we receive good at God’s hands, and not evil? Job 2:10. I am not utterly deserted, but only the case is a little altered, the right hand of the Most High alternated.
paragraphs.anchor: But I will remember, &c.

paragraphs.text: Remember, and commemorate, as the Hebrew (by a double reading) importeth.
paragraphs.anchor: I will remember the works, &c.

paragraphs.text: God is wonderful in counsel and excellent in working, Isa 28:29, and as we behold the sun in the waters, so God in his works. Saeculum speculum, the world is a glass or theatre, but especially the Church, wherein God setteth forth his wonders to the view of all.
paragraphs.anchor: I will remember thy wonders

paragraphs.text: {See Trapp on "Psa 45:1"}
paragraphs.anchor: I will meditate also of all thy works, and talk, &c.

paragraphs.text: There it is only that I can get satisfaction about thy proceedings, Psa 73:17. There I am taught, that thou art righteous in all thy ways, and holy in all thy works, Psa 145:17. Some render this text, Thy way, O God, is in holiness. Some by sanctuary understand heaven; q.d. Thy way is in heaven, far above man’s reach.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy way, O God, is in the sanctuary

paragraphs.text: And therefore no wonder his ways are so incomprehensible.
paragraphs.anchor: Who is so great a God as our God?

paragraphs.text: In the daily defence and government of thy Church. Thou art the great Thaumaturgus, or wonder worker.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou art the God that doest wonders

paragraphs.text: As among the Egyptians, Canaanites, Philistines, &c. Vere magnus est Dens Christianorum, said one Calocerius, a heathen.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast declared thy strength among the people

paragraphs.text: viz. Out of the bondage of Egypt, that memorable mercy; but nothing to that of ours and theirs from sin’s thraldom.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast with thine arm redeemed thy people

paragraphs.text: Joseph is instanced, quia nobilis inter fratres, vel in malis quae pendit, vel in bonis quae rependit, as Austin hath it (De Doct. Christ. 1. iv. c. 6).
paragraphs.anchor: The sons of Jacob and Joseph

paragraphs.text: The waters saw thee, O God … they were afraid] This is check to such as will not see to fear so mighty a God. "Lord," saith the prophet, "when thy hand is lifted up, they will not see; but they shall see and be ashamed for their envy at the people; yea, the fire of thine enemies shall devour them," Isa 26:11.

Calvin taketh this to be a description of that hideous tempest, Exo 9:18-26, the seventh plague of Egypt. But others with more probability hold, that the prophet here hath respect to that very time mentioned in the former verse, when the Lord looked upon the host of the Egyptians out of the fiery and cloudy pillar, and so troubled and turmoiled them with stormy tempests, that their chariot wheels fell off, and themselves sank as lead in the mighty waters, Exo 14:24-25; Exo 15:10. Of these terrible tempests mention is made also by Justin.
paragraphs.anchor: The clouds poured out water, the skies, &c.

paragraphs.text: Heb. in the sphere or round orb of the air. Of the thunder in the air, see Job 37:2-5 Psa 29:1-11 This made the Egyptians say, Let us flee, for God fighteth for Israel against us.
paragraphs.anchor: The voice of thy thunder was in the heaven

paragraphs.text: Such flakes of fire there were with flashes of lightning, as darkened the sun, and made the whole heaven seem to be on a light fire.
paragraphs.anchor: The lightnings lightened the world

paragraphs.text: A way of thine own miraculous making. God usually goeth a way by himself.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy way is in the sea, &c.

paragraphs.text: Not so much as is the way or an eagle in the air, the way of a serpent upon a rock, or the way of a ship in the midst of the sea, Pro 30:19. Let God alone with his own work, commit we ourselves to him in well doing, and it shall go well with us, no question of it. Pit viam desperatae salutis, impii foveam insperatae mortis intrant (Oros.).
paragraphs.anchor: And thy footsteps are not known

paragraphs.text: And so he still leadeth his Church with much love and care, by good magistrates and ministers, who are as his under-shepherds.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou leddest thy people like a flock
